questions.question: Maya wraps a string exactly once around a circular jar lid. She then cuts the string into pieces that are each exactly as long as the lid's diameter, which is 20 cm. She gets 3 whole pieces and one leftover piece about 2.8 cm long. For this lid, what is circumference ÷ diameter?
questions.explain: Three diameter-pieces plus a 2.8 cm leftover means the rim is 3 diameters plus 2.8 ÷ 20 = 0.14 of a diameter, so C ÷ d is about 3.14. A common trap is reading only the leftover (0.14) or rounding the 3 whole pieces up to 4 — the leftover is a small extra part of one diameter, not a whole one.

questions.question: A circle with a diameter of 10 cm is drawn on the board. Starting at one point, the teacher marks the rim into arcs that are each exactly 10 cm long, the same as the diameter. Three whole 10 cm arcs fit around the rim, and then a small leftover arc closes the circle. About how long is that leftover arc?
options: 0 cm — the three arcs close the circle exactly
questions.explain: Every circle's rim is about 3.14 diameters long, so with d = 10 cm the rim is about 31.4 cm: three 10 cm arcs use 30 cm and about 1.4 cm is left. The common mistake is thinking pi is exactly 3 so nothing is left over — there is always a small extra piece, about 0.14 of a diameter.

questions.question: A round drum lid has its rim divided into 6 equal arcs, each 5 cm long, so the whole rim is 30 cm. The diameter of the lid measures about 9.5 cm. About how many diameter-lengths long is the rim?
options: about 30 diameters, one for each centimetre
about 6 diameters, one for each arc
questions.explain: Compare the rim to the diameter: 30 ÷ 9.5 is about 3.2, so the rim is a little more than 3 diameters, just as C ÷ d is always about 3.14. A common trap is counting the 6 arcs instead — the arcs are 5 cm each, not one diameter each.

questions.question: A circular tabletop is cut in half by a line through its centre. The rim is made of 2 equal half-arcs, each 47 cm long, and the line across the middle measures 30 cm. Which value is closest to circumference ÷ diameter for this tabletop?
questions.explain: The whole rim is 47 + 47 = 94 cm and the line through the centre is the diameter, 30 cm, so 94 ÷ 30 is about 3.13 — close to pi as expected. Traps here are dividing only one half-arc by the diameter, or dividing by the radius (15 cm) instead of the diameter.

questions.question: A circular canoe hatch has a radius of 7 cm. Which calculation correctly finds the circumference of the hatch?
questions.explain: C = pi × d, and the diameter is twice the radius, so d = 14 cm and C = 3.14 × 14. The most common mistake is multiplying pi by the radius instead of the diameter, which gives only half the true circumference.

questions.question: Devan's bike wheel has a diameter of 60 cm. How far does the bike travel when the wheel makes exactly one full turn?
questions.explain: One full turn rolls out the circumference, so C = 3.14 × 60 = 188.4 cm. Watch for using the radius (30 cm) by mistake, which gives 94.2 cm — only half a turn's worth of distance.

questions.question: A hula hoop has a circumference of 220 cm. Which is closest to the diameter of the hoop?
questions.explain: Since C = pi × d, work backwards with d = 220 ÷ 3.14, which is about 70 cm. A common trap is halving the circumference (110 cm) — the rim is about 3.14 diameters long, not 2.

questions.question: Four students each measure a different round object and calculate circumference ÷ diameter. Which statement about that quotient is true for every circle?
options: It gets bigger as the circle gets bigger
It is about 2 for small circles and about 3 for large ones
It changes if you measure in metres instead of centimetres
It is always about 3.14, no matter the size of the circle
questions.explain: For every circle, big or small, the rim is about 3.14 diameters long, and that is the number we call pi. The trap is thinking a bigger circle gives a bigger quotient — a bigger circle has a bigger circumference AND a bigger diameter, so the ratio stays the same.

questions.question: A round trampoline in a Surrey backyard has a radius of 1.5 m. A family wants safety netting that goes all the way around the outside edge. The netting costs $12 per metre. How much will the netting cost?
questions.explain: First find the diameter, 1.5 × 2 = 3 m, then the distance around: C = 3.14 × 3 = 9.42 m, and 9.42 × 12 = $113.04. The usual trap is multiplying pi by the radius instead of the diameter, which gives 4.71 m and only about half the real cost.

questions.question: Jonah measures a circular pot lid with a string. He gets a circumference of 40 cm and a diameter of 13 cm, so 40 ÷ 13 is about 3.08. He says, 'That can't be right — it has to come out to exactly 3.14.' What is the best response to Jonah?
options: He is right — circumference ÷ diameter comes out to exactly 3.14 for every circle, so a result of 3.08 means he divided wrongly
His work is fine: string measuring is never perfect and pi is only about 3.14, so a result near 3.14, like 3.08, is expected
His lid must not be a true circle, because real circles always give exactly 3.14, and 3.08 shows the lid is slightly squashed
He should divide the diameter by the circumference instead, because the ratio for pi always puts the shorter length first
questions.explain: Pi is a decimal that never ends and never repeats, and real measurements always have small errors, so hand-measured circles give values near 3.14 such as 3.08 or 3.2. The misconception is treating 3.14 as an exact answer that every measurement must land on.

questions.question: A Vancouver pizza shop bakes on two circular pans. The small pan has a diameter of 30 cm and the large pan has a diameter of 45 cm. Both pizzas have crust all the way around the edge. How much MORE crust does the large pizza have around its edge than the small one?
questions.explain: Find each circumference with C = pi × d: 3.14 × 45 = 141.3 cm and 3.14 × 30 = 94.2 cm, so the difference is 47.1 cm. A common trap is subtracting the diameters first and stopping at 15 cm — that difference still has to be multiplied by pi to become crust length.

questions.question: Sana draws a circle with a diameter of 20 cm, then draws a bigger one with a diameter of 40 cm. She says, 'The circumference only grows by 3.14 cm, because pi gets added on.' Which statement correctly describes what happens, with the reason?
options: The circumference grows by exactly 3.14 cm, from 62.8 cm to 65.94 cm, because pi is added on
The circumference stays 62.8 cm, because pi is always 3.14 and never changes
The circumference becomes 4 times as long, from 62.8 cm to 251.2 cm, because both the width and height doubled
The circumference doubles, from 62.8 cm to 125.6 cm, because C = pi × d and the diameter doubled
questions.explain: In C = pi × d, pi is multiplied by the diameter, so doubling the diameter doubles the circumference: 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm becomes 3.14 × 40 = 125.6 cm. The misconception is treating pi as something added to the diameter rather than multiplied by it.
